rationale: The boundary receipt closes the last open question and closes it in the direction the source ordering predicted: with the tightest uniform configuration ValidateConfig accepts - election timeout one millisecond above the leader's lease - the separation held in all sixteen trials, no competing leader appeared during any confirmation window, and the leader stepped down in every trial. That puts the uniform-case bound on the direction of the inequality rather than on any slack in the timers, and leaves the mixed-timer configuration as the only path into the defect, now with both its sides measured.

interpretations.rationale: Retained execution (check 483b4ed81c5e4a2caedae35b8899165a, exit 0, tests_passed, 60 parsed events, 0 parse errors; sixteen hand-built four-node clusters whose nodes all carry heartbeat 50ms, election 51ms and lease 50ms). The declared control held and is complete over all sixteen results (indices 29, 31, 33, 35, 37, 39, 41, 43, 45, 47, 49, 51, 53, 55, 57, 59, each admitted by its own baseline event), with no witnesses of an overlap: no trial saw a competing leader appear while the cut-off leader was still confirming, the confirmations ran eighteen to twenty-one per trial and ended between 47ms and 56ms, and the leader stepped down in every trial. So the near-tie did not let a peer's timer win: the configured relation was election timeout 51ms against lease 50ms, and the lease still ended the window first in all sixteen runs. Together with the earlier work this fixes both sides of the boundary that the VerifyLeader finding depends on - a voter whose election timeout is below the leader's lease produces the overlap every time (twenty of twenty), and a voter whose election timeout is above it produces none even at a one-millisecond margin (sixteen of sixteen) - which is what makes the condition an inequality between configured values rather than a matter of timing slack. The question is answered and the boundary recorded.

knowledge.assertion: The entry calls the known-leader refusal the gate that produces the separation; this run shows it holds even when the configured margin between a peer's election timeout and the leader's lease is one millisecond.

counterevidence: One millisecond is the tightest margin tested; the direction is established with two configurations rather than swept across values, and a margin in the other direction by a similarly small amount was not run (the mixed case used 20ms against 50ms).
The trials start from a stable cluster with freshly reset follower timers, so the measured relation covers a partition applied to a quiet cluster rather than one landing during an election.
No application read is served, so what is measured is the absence of a competing leader during the confirmation window rather than a value handed to a client.
Both sides run in one process with in-memory transports, so the round-trip component of the ordering is that of a loopback transport.
limitations: One cluster shape (three voters plus one nonvoter, quorum two) and one transport, as in the rest of this family.

The poll interval bounds the appearance time of any competing leader at 2ms, which is coarser than the margin being tested; the observation that none appeared is therefore about the window as sampled, not a sub-millisecond claim.
The competing leader's absence is read from the two isolated nodes' states at poll time, and the loop stops as soon as the leader steps down.
